a: not left a handful of us alive
t: A few survivors, or a seed?
p: The Hebrew has 'a survivor, a few'. The Greek has 'a seed', and Paul quotes the Greek in Romans 9:29.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV, BSB
readings.orig: הוֹתִיר לָנוּ שָׂרִיד כִּמְעָט (hotir lanu sarid kim'at)
readings.en: left us a survivor, a few
readings.plain: not left a handful of us alive

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: left us a seed

why: The Hebrew is supported by the Great Isaiah Scroll and by every Hebrew witness. The Greek 'seed' is an interpretation: a few survivors are the seed from which a people can grow again, as in 6:13.
b: Paul quotes the verse in the Greek's words to say that God has kept a remnant of Israel who believe (Romans 9:27–29). The Greek translator may have been thinking of the 'holy seed' of 6:13, or of the promise to Abraham's seed.

a: I cannot stand wrongdoing and a sacred assembly together.
p: Where the Hebrew has 'wrongdoing and assembly', the Greek has 'fasting and idleness'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 4QIsa-f (4Q60); KJV, BSB
readings.en: I cannot bear wrongdoing and assembly
readings.plain: I cannot stand wrongdoing and a sacred assembly together.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: οὐκ ἀνέχομαι· νηστείαν καὶ ἀργίαν (ouk anechomai; nēsteian kai argian)
readings.en: I cannot bear (them): fasting and idleness
readings.plain: I cannot stand them: fasting and idleness.

why: All the Hebrew witnesses, including two scrolls, agree. The Greek translator seems to have read the line as a list of festivals: 'atsarah, a day when work stops, became 'idleness', and in place of 'aven, 'wrongdoing', he put 'fasting', which may be a free rendering or a different Hebrew word.
b: The Hebrew's point is the mix: worship and wrongdoing at the same time. The Greek makes it a rejection of the festivals themselves, which loses the edge of the Hebrew, though 1:14 says much the same.

p: The Great Isaiah Scroll adds 'your fingers with guilt', words found in Isaiah 59:3.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-f (4Q60); Greek; KJV, BSB
readings.en: your hands are full of blood

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: your hands are full of blood, your fingers with guilt
readings.plain: Blood fills your hands, and guilt your fingers.

why: The extra words match 59:3 ('your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with guilt'), and a copyist who knew that verse probably added them here. 4QIsa-f, the Greek and the other witnesses lack them.

a: those in her who turn back
p: The same Hebrew letters can be read 'her returners' (the Masoretic vowels) or 'her captivity' (the Greek).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) (same letters); BSB
readings.en: and her returning ones
readings.plain: those in her who turn back

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: her captivity, that is, her captives

why: The written letters wshbyh are the same in both readings; only the vowels differ. 'Those who turn back' (from shuv) fits the call to repent in 1:16–20 and the sinners of 1:28, who do not. 'Her captives' (from shavah) fits a later time of exile, and the Greek translator lived in one.
b: The KJV's 'her converts' is a third way of putting the Hebrew: those in Zion who turn to God. The verse is the key to the chapter: Zion's ransom comes through justice, and those who share in it are the ones who turn back.

p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads 'your strength ... your work', speaking to the hearers directly.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-f (4Q60), which preserves 'his work'; KJV, BSB
readings.en: the strong one ... and his work

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: your strength (or store) ... and your work

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: their strength

why: 4QIsa-f preserves 'his work', agreeing with the Masoretic Text (its word for 'the strong man' is lost). The scroll and the Greek each make the rare word chason into the common 'strength' and supply a pronoun, which looks like an attempt to ease a hard text.
b: Chason, 'strong', is found elsewhere only in Amos 2:9, of the Amorites who were strong as oaks, which fits the oaks of 1:29–30. The strong man and his work, probably his idols, catch fire together.

t: A line skipped in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks 'to the mountain of the LORD', probably a copying slip from one 'to' to the next.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-f (4Q60); 4QIsa-e (4Q59), whose spacing implies it; Greek; Micah 4:2; KJV, BSB
readings.en: to the mountain of the LORD, to the house

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: (no words here: 'let us go up to the house of the God of Jacob')

why: The phrase begins and ends with the same word, 'el, 'to', and a copyist's eye jumped from the first to the second. Every other witness has it, including the copy of the same oracle in Micah 4:2.

a: and you must not pardon them.
t: 2:9b–10 missing in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the last line of 2:9 and all of 2:10. Two Qumran fragments and the Greek have them.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, BSB
readings.en: and do not lift up (forgive) them
readings.plain: and you must not pardon them.

readings.w: 4QIsa-b (4Q56); 4QIsa-a (4Q55) preserves only the last word
readings.en: and you will not forgive them
readings.plain: and you will not pardon them.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: καὶ οὐ μὴ ἀνήσω αὐτούς (kai ou mē anēsō autous)
readings.en: and I will not forgive them
readings.plain: and I will not pardon them.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: (no words here)

why: Most scholars think the scroll's copyist skipped the lines, perhaps because 2:10 and 2:19–21 are so alike. Others think the words were added to the Hebrew later, since the command 'do not pardon them' is abrupt and 2:10 repeats 2:19. The Plain follows the Hebrew, which two other Qumran copies and the Greek support.
b: The two fragments, 4QIsa-a and 4QIsa-b, show that the longer text was already being copied at Qumran. 4QIsa-b reads velo', 'and not', a statement rather than the Masoretic command (ve'al), which agrees with the Greek's 'and I will not forgive them', where God is the speaker.

t: 2:10 missing in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: This whole verse is missing from the Great Isaiah Scroll (see the variant at 2:9).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-a (4Q55) and 4QIsa-b (4Q56); Greek; KJV, BSB
readings.en: go into the rock

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: (no words here)

why: Two other Qumran copies and the Greek have the verse, so the scroll's gap is probably a copying slip. The Greek adds at the end 'when he rises to shatter the earth', from 2:19 and 2:21.

t: A verse the Greek does not have
p: The Greek has no 2:22. The Great Isaiah Scroll has it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV, BSB
readings.en: cease for yourselves from humankind

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: (no words here)

why: The verse is in every Hebrew witness, including the Great Isaiah Scroll, so it was in the Hebrew by the second century BC. It may still be an addition to the poem: it speaks to the hearers in a new way and works as a heading for 3:1–9. The Greek translator may have left out a verse he found hard, or worked from a copy without it.

p: The Greek reads 'Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us'. Early Christians read it of Christ.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) ('to the righteous'); KJV, BSB
readings.en: say of the righteous that it is good

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: Δήσωμεν τὸν δίκαιον, ὅτι δύσχρηστος ἡμῖν ἐστιν (Dēsōmen ton dikaion, hoti dyschrēstos hēmin estin)
readings.en: Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us
readings.plain: Let us bind the righteous one, for he is no use to us.

why: The Greek translator read 'imru, 'say', as ne'esor, 'let us bind', and 'good' as 'not good for us'. The Hebrew is supported by the Great Isaiah Scroll and fits 3:11, its matching line on the wicked.
b: The Greek line had a long life. Wisdom of Solomon 2:12 echoes it in the plot of the wicked against the righteous man. The Epistle of Barnabas (6:7) and Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 17; 133; 136–137) quote it of the death of Jesus, and Hegesippus, as Eusebius reports, put it in the mouths of the men who killed James the brother of Jesus (Church History 2.23.15).

p: The Hebrew has nashim, 'women'. The Greek read the same letters as noshim, 'creditors'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV, BSB
readings.en: and women rule over him

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: οἱ ἀπαιτοῦντες κυριεύουσιν ὑμῶν (hoi apaitountes kyrieuousin hymōn)
readings.en: those who demand payment rule over you

why: The letters nshym can be 'women' or 'creditors, lenders', and the Greek line before has 'exactors' for 'a child'. The Hebrew vowels, the Great Isaiah Scroll, the Latin and most translations have 'women', which fits the scorn for weak rulers in 3:4 and leads into 3:16. Some modern scholars prefer 'creditors', since 3:14–15 is about the rich robbing the poor.

p: The Hebrew says 'the peoples'. The Greek and the Syriac have 'his people', which fits 3:14.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: to judge peoples

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus; Syriac Peshitta, as reported in BHS
readings.en: his people

why: The Hebrew is supported by the Great Isaiah Scroll, and 'his people' looks like a correction to suit 3:14, where the LORD judges the leaders of his own people. The KJV and BSB have 'the people', a third way of rendering the Hebrew.

a: a burn scar where beauty was.
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll adds boshet, 'shame', so the line reads 'for instead of beauty, shame'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: branding instead of beauty
readings.plain: a burn scar where beauty was.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); BSB
readings.en: for instead of beauty, shame

why: The Masoretic Text's short line, with ki as a rare noun 'branding', is the harder reading. The scroll's copyist probably took ki as 'for' and added a word to finish the sentence. Some modern versions follow the scroll.
b: The Greek lacks the whole last line. 'Branding' matches the KJV's 'burning instead of beauty' and the rough treatment of captives elsewhere (see the note).

p: The Greek has 'God will shine with counsel and glory on the earth', with no 'branch'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV, BSB
readings.en: the sprout of the LORD

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: ἐπιλάμψει ὁ θεὸς ἐν βουλῇ μετὰ δόξης (epilampsei ho theos en boulē meta doxēs)
readings.en: God will shine forth in counsel with glory
readings.plain: God will shine out in counsel

why: Every Hebrew witness has tsemach. The Greek translator seems to have taken the verb behind it in an Aramaic sense, 'shine', as the Greek does again at Zechariah 6:12, where the Branch is called Anatolē, 'Rising' (of the sun).
b: The Targum, by contrast, makes the branch the Messiah (see the note). The Greek reading leaves the verse without any figure of a person.

p: The Great Isaiah Scroll adds 'and Judah': 'the survivors of Israel and Judah'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Greek; KJV, BSB
readings.en: for the survivors of Israel

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: for the survivors of Israel and Judah
readings.plain: the survivors of Israel and Judah

why: Only the scroll has 'and Judah'. A copyist may have added it because the passage is about Jerusalem, so that 'Israel' would not be read as the northern kingdom alone.

p: The Great Isaiah Scroll has 'a spirit of storm' (sa'ar) for 'a spirit of burning' (ba'er).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Greek ('burning'); KJV, BSB
readings.en: and by a spirit of burning

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: and by a spirit (wind) of storm

why: The Greek agrees with the Masoretic Text. The scroll may have taken ruach as 'wind' and supplied the word that usually goes with it (ruach se'arah, 'storm wind', Psalm 148:8; Ezekiel 1:4).

a: He broke up its soil, picked out its stones
p: The Greek begins 'I put a hedge around it and fenced it', in the first person. Jesus' parable has the hedge.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); BSB
readings.en: and he dug it and cleared it of stones
readings.plain: He broke up its soil, picked out its stones

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus; KJV ('he fenced it')
readings.orig: καὶ φραγμὸν περιέθηκα καὶ ἐχαράκωσα (kai phragmon periethēka kai echarakōsa)
readings.en: and I put a hedge around it and fenced it with stakes
readings.plain: I put a hedge around it and fenced it in

why: 'Izzeq appears only here, and its meaning was guessed from early on: 'dig, hoe' (from later Hebrew) or 'fence in' (from an Aramaic word for a ring). The Greek and the KJV take it as fencing. The Plain follows the more likely sense, 'dig', since clearing stones is the next step in preparing a field.
b: Jesus' parable of the tenants begins with the Greek's words, "He set a hedge around it" (Matthew 21:33; Mark 12:1), so the Gospels follow the Greek of Isaiah here. The Greek also has the owner speak in the first person from the start.

p: The Greek has 'thorns' for the Hebrew's 'stinking grapes'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV ('wild grapes'), BSB ('sour')
readings.en: stinking things, rotten grapes

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: thorns

why: Every Hebrew witness has be'ushim. The Greek translator may not have known the rare word and supplied 'thorns' from 5:6, or wanted a clearer picture of a vineyard gone wrong.

p: The Hebrew has garim, 'foreigners, sojourners'. The Greek has 'lambs', and many scholars read 'young goats'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV, BSB
readings.en: sojourners, foreigners

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: lambs

why: The Hebrew is in all the Hebrew witnesses, including two scrolls. The Greek, and many modern scholars who suggest the similar gedayim, 'young goats', make the line match its first half, where lambs graze. The Plain keeps the Hebrew: after the city's fall, animals and foreigners alike feed in the ruins of the rich.

a: the hems of his robe filled the temple
p: The Greek has 'and the house was full of his glory'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV, BSB
readings.en: and his skirts filled the temple
readings.plain: the hems of his robe filled the temple

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: καὶ πλήρης ὁ οἶκος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ (kai plērēs ho oikos tēs doxēs autou)
readings.en: and the house was full of his glory
readings.plain: the house was full of his glory

why: The Hebrew is supported by the Great Isaiah Scroll. The Greek, like the Targum's 'the brightness of his glory', avoids describing God's clothing and repeats the 'glory' of 6:3.
b: The scroll also reads 'his throne' for 'a throne', a small difference that does not change the sense.

t: Two "holies" in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll has 'holy, holy', only twice. The Masoretic Text and the Greek have three.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Greek; Revelation 4:8; KJV, BSB
readings.en: holy, holy, holy

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: holy, holy

why: A copyist could easily drop one of three identical words, and the scroll has other slips of this kind (it writes 'six wings' once in 6:2, where the Hebrew repeats it). The threefold form is in the Masoretic Text, the Greek, the Targum and the songs that grew from the verse, the Jewish Kedushah and the Christian Sanctus; Revelation 4:8 has three.
b: The scroll also reads 'they call' (plural) and leaves out 'and said', which does not change the sense. Some scholars have argued that the double 'holy' was the older form, but few follow them.

t: "Do not" or "upon"? The Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll writes 'l with ayin, not aleph, twice in 6:9. Some read it as a different sense of the commission.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Greek ('you will not understand'); KJV, BSB
readings.en: and do not understand

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: perhaps 'and on this (or: because) you will understand'

why: The Masoretic Text, the Greek and every New Testament quotation have the negative. The scroll writes w'l with the letter ayin in both lines of 6:9 (also 'look and look' without 'and'), and in 6:10 it writes hšm for 'make fat' (hashmen). The scroll's Hebrew often confuses aleph and ayin, which were no longer clearly told apart in speech (Kutscher), so the change may be only spelling. Others, beginning with Brownlee, have argued that a scribe reworked the commission, so that the people are told to keep listening in order to understand, and that hšm should be read from shamem, 'make appalled'; Evans discusses the scroll's form of the passage at length. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.
b: If the change is deliberate, it is the oldest known attempt to soften the hardening of 6:9–10, older than the Greek's softening and the New Testament's use of it.

p: The Hebrew commands 'Make ... fat'. The Greek says 'this people's heart has grown fat', and Matthew and Acts quote the Greek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, BSB
readings.en: make fat the heart of this people

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus; Matthew 13:15; Acts 28:27
readings.orig: ἐπαχύνθη γὰρ ἡ καρδία τοῦ λαοῦ τούτου (epachynthē gar hē kardia tou laou toutou)
readings.en: for the heart of this people has grown fat
readings.plain: For this people's heart has grown fat,

why: The Masoretic Text has the commands of 6:9–10; the Great Isaiah Scroll's different letters here are discussed in the variant at 6:9. The Greek turns them into statements: the people have dulled themselves, and the prophet's task is to say so. It softens a hard text that the Hebrew allows no way around.
b: Matthew 13:14–15 and Acts 28:26–27 quote the Greek, so the people are blamed for closing their own eyes. John 12:40 follows neither exactly and makes God the one who blinds. Mark 4:12 is close to the Targum (see the next variant).

p: The Hebrew ends 'and be healed'. The Targum has 'and it be forgiven them', as Mark 4:12 does.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); Greek ('and I will heal them'); KJV, BSB
readings.en: and one heal him

readings.w: Targum of Isaiah, as translated by Chilton
readings.en: and it be forgiven them

why: The Targum explains the picture: healing means forgiveness. The Hebrew and Greek have 'heal'.
b: Mark's form of the saying ends "and be forgiven" (Mark 4:12), against both the Hebrew and the Greek. Many scholars take this as a sign that the saying of Jesus was shaped by the Aramaic reading of Isaiah used in synagogues, which later took written form in the Targum.

a: Its stump is a holy seed.
t: A line the Greek does not have
p: The Greek lacks 'Its stump is a holy seed'. The Great Isaiah Scroll has it, as 'the holy seed'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) ('the holy seed'); KJV, BSB
readings.en: a holy seed is its stump
readings.plain: Its stump is a holy seed.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: (no words here)

why: The line is in the Great Isaiah Scroll, from the second century BC, so it is old. The Greek ends the verse with the acorn falling from its husk, perhaps because the translator's eye skipped from one matsevet, 'stump', to the second, or because his Hebrew lacked the line. Many critical scholars think the line was added after the exile; others think it is original.
b: The scroll also has two different words earlier in the verse (see the note on 'And though a tenth is still left in it').
